qs.q: Why do some students find it hard to stay motivated at school?
qs.a: Well, I'd say it's mostly because lessons can feel disconnected from real life. If pupils can't see why algebra matters, they switch off. For example, my cousin hated maths until a teacher showed him how engineers use it to design bridges. After that, he started working harder. So relevance is the key, I think.

qs.q: Do you think exams are the best way to measure what a student knows?
qs.a: Not really, to be honest. Exams test memory under pressure, which isn't the same as understanding. A student might panic and forget everything. That said, they're fair and simple to organise. On the whole, I'd prefer a mix, such as exams plus projects, so that different strengths can show up.

qs.q: How important is the teacher's personality in the classroom?
qs.a: I'd say it's very important. A friendly, patient teacher makes students feel safe to ask questions, and that boosts learning. I remember a geography teacher who told funny stories about every country. We all paid attention and remembered the facts. Knowledge matters, of course, but personality is what keeps the lesson alive.

qs.q: Should schools teach practical skills like cooking or managing money?
qs.a: Yes, definitely. Many young adults leave school knowing history dates but not how to budget a monthly salary. Teaching basic finance would prevent a lot of stress later, for instance with credit cards or rent. On the whole, I think schools should prepare pupils for life, not only for exams, so these lessons would be really valuable.

qs.q: How has technology changed the way people communicate?
qs.a: Well, it has made communication much faster and cheaper. Twenty years ago, you waited weeks for a letter from abroad; now you can video-call your brother in seconds. That said, I think conversations have become shallower. People send short messages instead of talking properly. So we gained speed, but perhaps we lost some depth.

qs.q: Do you think people depend too much on their phones?
qs.a: Yes, I'd say so. Many people check their phone every few minutes without even noticing. At restaurants, you often see a whole family looking at screens instead of talking. It's convenient, of course, but this habit can harm concentration and relationships. On the whole, we should set limits, like keeping phones away during meals.

qs.q: Is it a good idea for young children to use tablets?
qs.a: In moderation, yes. Educational apps can teach letters and numbers in a fun way. However, too much screen time can affect sleep and attention. For example, a neighbour's child now struggles to sit still for a story. I'd say parents should choose the content carefully and limit use to about an hour daily.

qs.q: What new technology would you like to see in the next ten years?
qs.a: I'd love to see cheap, reliable translation devices that work offline. Imagine travelling anywhere and speaking naturally with local people. This would help students, tourists and workers alike. For instance, a patient could explain symptoms to a foreign doctor easily. On the whole, I believe such tools would bring people closer together.

qs.q: What makes a job satisfying, in your opinion?
qs.a: Well, I'd say feeling useful matters most. A good salary is important, but if you feel your work helps people, you go home happier. For example, a nurse I know earns an average wage, yet she loves her job because patients thank her every day. So purpose, respect and fair pay together create satisfaction.

qs.q: Do you think people should change jobs often?
qs.a: It depends. Changing jobs can teach you new skills and raise your salary. However, moving too often may look unreliable to employers. On the whole, I'd say staying three to five years is sensible: long enough to learn properly, short enough to keep growing. My uncle did exactly that and built a strong career.

qs.q: Is working from home better than working in an office?
qs.a: Each has advantages. At home, you save time on travelling and can concentrate quietly. That said, you miss the chance to chat and solve problems quickly with colleagues. A friend of mine felt lonely after a year at home. I think a hybrid system, two days at home and three in the office, works best.

qs.q: How can employers keep their staff happy?
qs.a: Well, fair pay is the starting point, but it isn't everything. Employers should listen to staff and offer chances to learn new skills. For example, a company that pays for training courses shows it values its people. Also, flexible hours help parents. On the whole, respect keeps employees loyal more than money alone.

qs.q: Who should be responsible for protecting the environment, individuals or governments?
qs.a: I'd say both, but governments carry the bigger responsibility. Individuals can recycle or save water, which helps, but only governments can pass laws that force factories to stop polluting. For instance, a ban on plastic bags changed habits in my city overnight. So people should act, yet strong rules make the real difference.

qs.q: Why do some people not care about environmental problems?
qs.a: Well, probably because the damage often feels distant. If your street is clean, a melting glacier seems unimportant. Also, daily problems like rent and prices take priority. That said, when people see the effects locally, such as a polluted river, they start caring. So I think education and visible examples are really needed.

qs.q: Do you think it is realistic to ask people to use less energy?
qs.a: Yes, if it's made easy and rewarding. Telling people to sacrifice comfort rarely works. However, offering cheaper bills for energy-saving lamps or good insulation does. For example, my neighbours installed solar panels once the government gave a discount. On the whole, small incentives work better than strict warnings.

qs.q: How can cities become greener?
qs.a: Well, planting more trees and creating parks would be a simple start. Cities could also encourage cycling with safe lanes and reduce car traffic in the centre. For example, some European cities have closed central streets to cars, and the air became cleaner. I'd say green spaces also make residents healthier and happier.

qs.q: Why do so many people move from villages to big cities?
qs.a: Mainly for jobs and opportunities. Cities offer better universities, hospitals and a wider choice of work. For example, many young people from small towns in my country go to the capital to find a good position. That said, they often face high rents. On the whole, hope for a better future drives the move.

qs.q: What are the main problems of living in a large city?
qs.a: Well, I'd say traffic and housing costs come first. Commuting can take two hours a day, which is exhausting. Also, noise and pollution affect health. A friend of mine pays half his salary on a tiny flat. So, although cities are exciting, life there can be stressful and expensive.

qs.q: Do you think old buildings should be protected or replaced with modern ones?
qs.a: I'd say the important ones should be protected, because they tell the story of a city. Tourists visit old streets, not glass towers. That said, if a building is dangerous or empty, replacing it makes sense. For example, an old market near me became a lovely library. So, a balance is best.

qs.q: How can a city make life better for its elderly residents?
qs.a: Well, simple things help a lot, such as benches in the street, ramps and clear signs. Cheap buses and nearby clinics matter too. For instance, my grandmother stopped going out when the pavement near her house was broken. After repairs, she walked to the shop again. On the whole, small details change older people's independence.

qs.q: Why do many people find it difficult to lead a healthy lifestyle?
qs.a: Well, I'd say it's largely about time and habit. People work long hours, so they grab fast food and skip exercise. Also, unhealthy snacks are cheap and everywhere. For example, my colleague wants to lose weight but eats lunch at his desk every day. So changing routine, not knowledge, is the real challenge.

qs.q: Is prevention more important than treatment?
qs.a: Definitely, in my view. Preventing illness is cheaper and less painful than curing it. For example, regular check-ups can detect high blood pressure before it causes a heart attack. That said, we obviously still need good hospitals. On the whole, governments should spend more on health education and screening programmes.

qs.q: Do you think mental health is taken seriously enough?
qs.a: Not yet, I'd say. Many people still feel ashamed to admit they are anxious or depressed, so they suffer silently. A friend of mine waited two years before speaking to a specialist. That said, awareness is growing. On the whole, schools and workplaces should talk about it openly to remove the stigma.

qs.q: Should unhealthy food be taxed?
qs.a: I think it could help, to be honest. A higher price on sugary drinks makes people think twice before buying them, and the money could fund hospitals. That said, the tax must not hurt poor families. For instance, healthy options should become cheaper at the same time. On the whole, it's worth trying.

qs.q: How has family life changed in the last few decades?
qs.a: Well, families are generally smaller now, and many parents both work. Fifty years ago, grandparents often lived in the same house, but today relatives may be in different cities. For example, my aunt raises her children alone because her family lives far away. So, we have more independence but less daily support.

qs.q: Is it better for children to be brought up in a big family?
qs.a: I'd say there are real benefits. Children learn to share, negotiate and help each other. For instance, in my family the older kids look after the younger ones, which teaches responsibility. That said, parents of large families have less time and money for each child. On the whole, it depends on the circumstances.

qs.q: What can parents do to stay close to their teenage children?
qs.a: Well, the key is listening without judging. Teenagers close up if every conversation becomes a lecture. Parents could share activities, like cooking or watching a match together. For example, my friend's father took him fishing every weekend, and they still talk openly today. On the whole, regular time together builds trust.

qs.q: Do you think grandparents should help raise grandchildren?
qs.a: Yes, within limits. Grandparents offer love, patience and stories that parents sometimes lack time for. For instance, my grandfather taught me proverbs and how to play chess. That said, the parents must stay in charge of the main rules. On the whole, it's a wonderful bond if everyone respects each other's role.

qs.q: Do you think people trust the news less nowadays?
qs.a: Yes, I'd say so. With social media, anyone can publish a story, and false information spreads quickly. For example, I recently saw a fake report about a food shortage that made people panic in the shops. That said, reliable newspapers still exist. On the whole, readers must check the source before believing a headline.

qs.q: How does advertising influence what people buy?
qs.a: Well, it influences us more than we admit. Adverts create the feeling that we need a product, often by linking it to happiness. For instance, a sports shoe advert shows a smiling champion, so people imagine they will run faster too. So I'd say we should ask ourselves whether we truly need the item.

qs.q: Should there be limits on what children can watch on screens?
qs.a: Yes, I think so. Some programmes show violence or unrealistic lifestyles that confuse young minds. Parents can use filters and choose suitable channels. For example, my sister lets her son watch nature documentaries but not action films. That said, banning everything doesn't work; discussing what they see is also important.

qs.q: Is it a good idea for famous people to share their private lives online?
qs.a: Not always. It can make them feel closer to their fans, but it also removes their privacy and pushes them to behave for attention. For example, some celebrities post every meal and then face harsh criticism. On the whole, I'd say keeping a part of life private is healthier.

qs.q: Why do people enjoy travelling to foreign countries?
qs.a: Well, I think curiosity is the main reason. People want to see new landscapes, taste different food and experience another way of life. For instance, a friend of mine returned from Turkey full of stories about its markets and history. That said, travelling also helps us relax and escape routine for a while.

qs.q: Do you think tourism is good for local communities?
qs.a: Mostly yes, because it creates jobs in hotels, restaurants and transport. However, it can raise prices and damage nature. For example, a quiet fishing village I visited became crowded and expensive after it became famous. On the whole, tourism helps if the number of visitors is managed carefully.

qs.q: Is it better to travel with a group or alone?
qs.a: I'd say it depends on your personality. In a group, you share costs and feel safe, which is great for a first trip. That said, travelling alone gives complete freedom to choose your schedule and meet local people. Personally, I'd prefer a small group of friends, so there's company and flexibility.

qs.q: How might travel change in the future?
qs.a: Well, I expect it to become more eco-friendly. Airlines are already testing cleaner fuels, and trains are improving. Also, virtual reality may let people preview a destination before booking. For instance, you could walk through a hotel from your sofa. On the whole, I think travelling will be easier, but perhaps more expensive.

qs.q: Do you think young people today are good at managing money?
qs.a: Not always, I'd say. Online shopping and easy payments make spending effortless, so many young people run out of money before the end of the month. For example, my cousin bought a new phone on credit and then struggled with the instalments. That said, some are quite smart and save regularly.

qs.q: Is it important to save money for the future?
qs.a: Absolutely. Life is unpredictable, and savings give you security if you lose your job or face a medical emergency. For instance, my neighbour could repair his flooded kitchen without borrowing because he had saved for years. On the whole, even small amounts every month make a big difference.

qs.q: Does having more money make people happier?
qs.a: Up to a point, yes. Money removes worries about food, rent and healthcare, which obviously improves life. However, beyond that, relationships and health matter more. For example, a wealthy relative of mine works constantly and seems exhausted. So I'd say money helps, but it can't replace time with loved ones.

qs.q: Should rich people pay higher taxes?
qs.a: Generally, I think yes, because they can afford it and society benefits from better schools and hospitals. That said, the system must be fair and transparent, so people trust where the money goes. For example, citizens accept taxes more willingly when they see new roads. On the whole, fairness and openness matter most.
